knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = FALSE, message = FALSE, warning = FALSE, fig.align = "center")
knitr::opts_knit$set(root.dir = normalizePath(".."))

```{r load}
suppressPackageStartupMessages({ library(dplyr); library(readr); library(knitr) })
res <- function(f) read_csv(file.path("results", f), show_col_types = FALSE)
qc   <- res("qc_subject.csv")
uni  <- res("channel_band_stats.csv")
lmmA <- res("lmm_anova.csv")
lmmR <- res("lmm_group_by_region.csv")
apfs <- res("alpha_peak_stats.csv")
clf  <- res("classifier_summary.csv")
coefs <- res("classifier_coefs.csv")
flags <- res("qc_channel_flags.csv")
fmt_p <- function(p) ifelse(p < .001, formatC(p, format = "e", digits = 1), sprintf("%.3f", p))
en <- filter(clf, grepl("Elastic", model)); bs <- filter(clf, grepl("Baseline", model))
ra <- filter(uni, measure == "rel", band == "alpha")
fig <- function(f) knitr::include_graphics(file.path("..", "figures", f), error = FALSE)
```

## Question

Is resting, eyes-closed EEG spectral power different in adolescents with
schizophrenia-spectrum disorders compared with healthy adolescents, in which
frequency bands and where on the scalp, and how well do these differences
separate the two groups out of sample?

## Data

The MSU adolescent schizophrenia EEG database (Borisov et al., 2005):
`r sum(qc$group == "Control")` healthy schoolboys and `r sum(qc$group == "Schizophrenia")`
boys with schizophrenia-spectrum diagnoses (ICD-10 F20, F21, F25), aged about 11 to 14,
unmedicated at the time of recording. Each record is 60 s of wakeful, eyes-closed EEG
from 16 scalp electrodes (10-20 system, linked-ear reference), sampled at 128 Hz and supplied
as artefact-free segments. Source: <http://brain.bio.msu.ru/eeg_schizophrenia.htm>.

## Methods

**Cleaning and QC.** Each channel was mean-centred. Recordings were checked for missing
values and flat channels (none). The 60 s were split into 29 overlapping 4-s segments, and a
segment was rejected if any channel's peak-to-peak amplitude exceeded that channel's
within-subject median + 5 MAD. Median rejected segments per subject:
`r median(qc$segments_rejected)` (max `r max(qc$segments_rejected)` of 29), so no subject met the
pre-specified exclusion rule (> 25% rejected). `r nrow(flags)` channel recordings had
outlying overall variance (|robust z| > 3.5, from `r n_distinct(flags$subject)` subjects); they were
kept, because log band power absorbs gain differences and the data were supplied as clean.

**Spectra and features.** Welch PSD per channel (4-s Hann windows, 50% overlap, linear detrend,
0.25 Hz resolution). Band power was integrated over delta (1-4 Hz), theta (4-8), alpha (8-13) and
beta (13-30), and expressed as **log10 absolute power** and **relative power** (share of 1-30 Hz).
Individual **alpha peak frequency** was the maximum of the mean posterior spectrum (O1, O2, P3, P4, Pz)
between 7 and 13 Hz, refined by parabolic interpolation; `r sum(is.na(read_csv(file.path("results","alpha_peak.csv"), show_col_types = FALSE)$alpha_peak_hz))`
adolescents whose maximum sat on the 7 Hz edge (no identifiable peak) were left out of that test.

**Statistics.** For each of 16 channels x 4 bands x 2 measures: Welch t-test, with a Wilcoxon
rank-sum test as a robustness check, and Hedges' *g* with 95% CI (schizophrenia minus control).
P-values were corrected with Benjamini-Hochberg FDR within each measure (64 tests). For a
region-level view, a linear mixed model per band,
`log10 power ~ group * region + (1 | subject)` (sum contrasts, Type III, Satterthwaite df; `lmerTest`).

**Classifier.** Elastic-net logistic regression (`glmnet`, alpha = 0.5) on all 128 band-power
features, with lambda chosen by inner 5-fold CV inside each outer training fold (nested CV;
standardisation learned on the training fold only). Performance: 10 x repeated stratified 5-fold
CV. Baseline: logistic regression on one feature, mean relative alpha across channels.
Significance: 200 label permutations of the full pipeline.

## Results

### Power spectra

```{r fig1, out.width = "100%"}
fig("fig1_power_spectra.png")
```

The healthy group shows the expected posterior alpha peak; in the schizophrenia group it is
lower and shifted to slower frequencies, while delta and theta power look similar.

### Channel-by-band effect sizes

```{r fig2, out.width = "100%"}
fig("fig2_effect_size_heatmap.png")
```

```{r tab-sig}
uni |>
  group_by(Measure = ifelse(measure == "rel", "Relative", "Log absolute"), Band = band) |>
  summarise(`Channels FDR q<.05 (t-test)` = sum(p_fdr < .05),
            `Channels FDR q<.05 (Wilcoxon)` = sum(p_wilcox_fdr < .05),
            `Hedges g range` = sprintf("%.2f to %.2f", min(g), max(g)), .groups = "drop") |>
  mutate(Band = factor(Band, c("delta", "theta", "alpha", "beta"))) |>
  arrange(Measure, Band) |>
  kable()
```

- **Alpha is reduced** in schizophrenia: lower absolute alpha at
  `r sum(uni$measure == "abs_log10" & uni$band == "alpha" & uni$p_fdr < .05)` of 16 channels and lower
  relative alpha at `r sum(ra$p_fdr < .05)` of 16. The largest effect is relative alpha at O1
  (g = `r sprintf("%.2f", ra$g[ra$channel == "O1"])`, 95% CI `r sprintf("%.2f to %.2f", ra$g_lo[ra$channel == "O1"], ra$g_hi[ra$channel == "O1"])`).
- **Absolute delta and theta do not differ** (all |g| < 0.36, none significant), so the higher
  *relative* delta and theta in schizophrenia mostly reflects the smaller alpha share, not extra
  slow-wave power. The relative delta/theta effects are less robust to the rank-based test.
- **Beta** trends lower in absolute terms (one channel, P3, survives FDR).

```{r fig3, out.width = "100%"}
fig("fig3_scalp_effect_maps.png")
```

### Region-level mixed models

```{r tab-lmm}
lmmA |>
  filter(term %in% c("group", "group:region")) |>
  transmute(Band = band, Term = term, `F` = sprintf("%.2f", F),
            df = sprintf("%d, %.0f", num_df, den_df), p = fmt_p(p),
            `FDR q (group)` = ifelse(is.na(p_fdr_group), "", fmt_p(p_fdr_group))) |>
  kable()
```

```{r tab-region}
lmmR |>
  filter(band == "alpha") |>
  transmute(Region = region, `Power ratio SCZ/CTL` = sprintf("%.2f", ratio),
            `Hedges g [95% CI]` = sprintf("%.2f [%.2f, %.2f]", g, g_lo, g_hi),
            `FDR q` = fmt_p(p_fdr)) |>
  kable(caption = "Absolute alpha power by region (region-averaged log10 power)")
```

Only alpha shows a main effect of group after FDR. Group x region interactions are significant
in every band, i.e. the group difference is not uniform over the scalp: for alpha it is largest
over occipital and frontal sites, where the schizophrenia group has roughly 45-60% of control alpha power.

```{r fig4, out.width = "100%"}
fig("fig4_relative_power_by_region.png")
```

### Alpha peak frequency

```{r fig5, out.width = "80%"}
fig("fig5_alpha_peak_frequency.png")
```

Mean alpha peak was `r sprintf("%.2f", apfs$mean_control)` Hz (SD `r sprintf("%.2f", apfs$sd_control)`)
in controls and `r sprintf("%.2f", apfs$mean_scz)` Hz (SD `r sprintf("%.2f", apfs$sd_scz)`) in the
schizophrenia group: Welch t(`r sprintf("%.1f", apfs$df)`) = `r sprintf("%.2f", apfs$t)`,
p = `r fmt_p(apfs$p)`, g = `r sprintf("%.2f [%.2f, %.2f]", apfs$g, apfs$g_lo, apfs$g_hi)`.

### Classification

```{r fig6, out.width = "100%"}
fig("fig6_classifier.png")
```

```{r tab-clf}
clf |>
  transmute(Model = model,
            `AUC mean (range over repeats)` = sprintf("%.2f (%.2f-%.2f)", auc_mean, auc_min, auc_max),
            `Balanced accuracy` = sprintf("%.2f", bal_acc_mean),
            `Permutation p` = ifelse(is.na(perm_p), "", sprintf("%.3f", perm_p))) |>
  kable()
```

The elastic net reached a cross-validated AUC of `r sprintf("%.2f", en$auc_mean)`, well above
the permutation null (95th percentile `r sprintf("%.2f", en$perm_null_95)`; none of 200 permutations
reached the observed value), but only slightly better than the single global-relative-alpha
feature (AUC `r sprintf("%.2f", bs$auc_mean)`). The most consistently selected features were
`r paste(head(coefs$feature, 5), collapse = ", ")`: alpha again carries most of the signal.

## Interpretation

Unmedicated adolescents with schizophrenia-spectrum disorders show a **reduced and slower
alpha rhythm** at rest, with otherwise similar absolute slow-wave power. This sits alongside the original authors' report, in this same
sample, of altered alpha-segment structure and reduced structural synchrony of alpha activity;
here the effect shows up in plain spectral power as well. A spectral
signature like this separates groups at roughly 70% balanced accuracy, which is useful for
research but nowhere near a diagnostic test.

## Limitations

- Small, single-site, all-male sample from one 2005 database; no age, IQ or symptom data per subject,
  so age (which strongly shapes alpha frequency in adolescence) cannot be modelled directly. The
  authors report matched mean ages (12.3 years in both groups).
- 60 s per subject; recordings were pre-selected as artefact-free by the data providers.
- The amplitude scale in the files is larger than typical scalp EEG in microvolts, so absolute
  power is reported on a log scale and interpreted only relative to the other group; relative
  power and peak frequency are unaffected by gain.
- 50 Hz is barely visible in the spectra, which suggests the data were low-pass filtered before
  sharing; analysis was restricted to 1-30 Hz.
- No licence is stated on the source page; the data are not redistributed here.

## Reference

Borisov SV, Kaplan AYa, Gorbachevskaya NL, Kozlova IA (2005). Analysis of EEG structural
synchrony in adolescents with schizophrenic disorders. *Human Physiology* 31(3):255-261.
<https://doi.org/10.1007/s10747-005-0042-z>
